# Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms

Journal: Computer Speech and Language

Wolfgang Mack Email: <wolfgang.mack@audiolabs-erlangen.de> Corresponding

Address: Friedrich-Alexander-University Erlangen-Nuremberg, Schloßplatz
4, 91054 Erlangen, Germany.    Emanuël A. P. Habets

###### Abstract

The [DOA](#id1) ([DOA](#id1)) of sound sources is an essential acoustic
parameter used, e.g., for multi-channel speech enhancement or source
tracking. Complex acoustic scenarios consisting of sources-of-interest,
interfering sources, reverberation, and noise make the estimation of the
[DOA](#id1)s corresponding to the sources-of-interest a challenging
task. Recently proposed attention mechanisms allow [DOA](#id1)
estimators to focus on the sources-of-interest and disregard
interference and noise, i.e., they are signal-aware. The attention is
typically obtained by a [DNN](#id6) ([DNN](#id6)) from a [STFT](#id4)
([STFT](#id4)) based representation of a single microphone signal.
Subsequently, attention has been applied as binary or ratio weighting to
[STFT](#id4)-based microphone signal representations to reduce the
impact of frequency bins dominated by noise, interference, or
reverberation. The impact of attention on [DOA](#id1) estimators and
different training strategies for attention and [DOA](#id1) [DNN](#id6)s
are not yet studied in depth. In this paper, we evaluate systems
consisting of different [DNN](#id6)s and signal processing-based methods
for [DOA](#id1) estimation when attention is applied. Additionally, we
propose training strategies for attention-based [DOA](#id1) estimation
optimized via a [DOA](#id1) objective, i.e., end-to-end. The evaluation
of the proposed and the baseline systems is performed using data
generated with simulated and measured room impulse responses under
various acoustic conditions, like reverberation times, noise, and source
array distances. The best-performing systems are also evaluated using
measured data. Our experiments show that [DNN](#id6)s used for
[DOA](#id1) estimation are biased to the spectral source characteristics
and the spectral attention distribution used during training (e.g.,
spectrally flat/sparse). We also show that this bias in the [DOA](#id1)
estimator can be avoided if signal-processing methods are used in
combination with attention. Overall, [DOA](#id1) estimation using
attention in combination with signal-processing methods exhibits a far
lower computational complexity than a fully [DNN](#id6)-based system;
however, it yields comparable results.

## 1 Introduction

The sound emitted by a point source in an enclosed space spreads
spherically and gets reflected by walls and other obstacles. Typically,
the non-reflected sound is referred to as direct, whereas reflections
are referred to as reverberation. Additional interfering sources like a
ventilator, or background noise, e.g., from a nearby road, add further
complexity to the sound field and severely degrade humans’ and machines’
ability to localize sources or understand speech. When such a sound
field is captured with an array of microphones, acoustic
signal-processing techniques can be used to increase the speech
intelligibility, e.g., with beamformers \[[1](#bib.bib1),
[2](#bib.bib2), [3](#bib.bib3), [4](#bib.bib4), [5](#bib.bib5)\], or to
track sources \[[6](#bib.bib6)\], e.g., with acoustic simultaneous
localization and mapping \[[7](#bib.bib7)\]. These techniques often
require estimates of the [DOA](#id1) of the sound sources. For some
applications, only the [DOA](#id1) of the [SOI](#id5) ([SOI](#id5)) is
desired or required. For example, consider two concurrently active
sources: [SOI](#id5) and interference. Conventional [DOA](#id1)
estimators yield the [DOA](#id1) of both sources. Typically, it is
unclear which of both [DOA](#id1)s corresponds to the [SOI](#id5) and
which to the interfering source. A correct [DOA](#id1) assignment to the
[SOI](#id5) is crucial for beamformers, as a wrong assignment leads to
an attenuation of the [SOI](#id5).

Estimation methods for the [DOA](#id1) have been investigated thoroughly
in the literature (e.g., \[[8](#bib.bib8), [9](#bib.bib9),
[10](#bib.bib10)\]). Typically, [DOA](#id1) estimators exploit spatial
features present in the microphone signals due to a level difference and
a time difference of arrival (TDOA) of the source signal between the
individual microphones. For far-field scenarios and omnidirectional
microphones, the level difference is usually minimal and can be
neglected. In the frequency domain, the TDOA translates to
frequency-band specific phase-differences between the microphones. Here,
the spatial features can be exploited per frequency band (narrowband) or
from all frequency bands (broadband). Signal processing-based methods to
estimate the [DOA](#id1) from these features can be based on the
inter-microphone cross-correlations \[[11](#bib.bib11),
[12](#bib.bib12), [13](#bib.bib13)\], beamformers \[[14](#bib.bib14),
[15](#bib.bib15), [16](#bib.bib16)\] or subspaces \[[17](#bib.bib17),
[16](#bib.bib16), [18](#bib.bib18), [19](#bib.bib19), [20](#bib.bib20),
[21](#bib.bib21), [22](#bib.bib22)\]. The inter-microphone
cross-correlations, like the generalized-cross-correlation
\[[23](#bib.bib23)\] with maximum likelihood or phase transform (PHAT)
\[[13](#bib.bib13)\] weighting exploit the [DOA](#id1) and frequency
dependency of the inter-microphone phase-differences to estimate the
[DOA](#id1). In \[[24](#bib.bib24)\], a least square approach is used to
minimize the phase differences obtained from measurements and an
estimated [DOA](#id1). Beamforming techniques like steered-response
power, e.g., with PHAT weighting \[[15](#bib.bib15), [16](#bib.bib16)\]
(SRP-P), or a steered minimum-variance distortionless response
beamformer \[[14](#bib.bib14)\] sample the [DOA](#id1) space by steering
in pre-defined directions. The [DOA](#id1) is subsequently estimated by
maximum picking. An alternative is null-steering \[[25](#bib.bib25)\],
where the idea is similar, but the [DOA](#id1) is obtained by minimum
picking. Alternatively, the [DOA](#id1) can be estimated using
subspace-based methods like MUltiple SIgnal Classification (MUSIC)
\[[17](#bib.bib17), [16](#bib.bib16), [18](#bib.bib18)\], based on noise
subspaces, or estimation of signal parameters via rotational invariant
techniques \[[19](#bib.bib19), [20](#bib.bib20), [21](#bib.bib21),
[22](#bib.bib22)\], based on sub-arrays. In \[[26](#bib.bib26)\], the
authors exploit reflection patterns using semi-supervised manifold
learning with a distributed microphone array to localize a single
source.

Also, deep-learning techniques have been used for [DOA](#id1) estimation
\[[27](#bib.bib27), [28](#bib.bib28), [29](#bib.bib29),
[30](#bib.bib30), [31](#bib.bib31), [32](#bib.bib32), [33](#bib.bib33),
[34](#bib.bib34), [35](#bib.bib35), [36](#bib.bib36), [37](#bib.bib37),
[38](#bib.bib38), [39](#bib.bib39), [40](#bib.bib40), [41](#bib.bib41),
[42](#bib.bib42), [43](#bib.bib43), [44](#bib.bib44), [45](#bib.bib45),
[46](#bib.bib46), [47](#bib.bib47), [48](#bib.bib48), [49](#bib.bib49),
[50](#bib.bib50), [51](#bib.bib51)\]. Typically, deep-learning methods
for [DOA](#id1) estimation are computationally more complex than
signal-processing methods and require retraining or architecture
modifications if fundamental parameters like the number of microphones
or the array architecture change. When using deep learning for
[DOA](#id1) estimation, a [DNN](#id6) learns to map a feature
representation of the microphone signals to the [DOA](#id1). This
enables matching the trained [DNN](#id6) via the training data to
specific scenarios. The estimated [DOA](#id1) on the [DNN](#id6) output
can be represented in a classification manner, where a class activity
symbolizes an active source from the corresponding direction, or a
regression manner, where a single variable represents the [DOA](#id1)
(e.g., an angle). According to \[[28](#bib.bib28)\], both
representations yield comparable results such that the output
representation of the [DOA](#id1) is a design choice. Some of the
[DNN](#id6)s for [DOA](#id1) estimation (referred to as DDNNs) are
trained with directional noise signals (e.g., \[[40](#bib.bib40),
[45](#bib.bib45), [52](#bib.bib52)\]) as this allows to generate an
infinite amount of simulated training data. Conceptually, training with
noise implies that the DDNN learns spatial and no spectral source
characteristics, as expected of a [DOA](#id1) estimator. Very recently,
\[[53](#bib.bib53)\] showed that training with speech improves the
localization of speech sources compared to training with noise, although
the DDNN was only provided with the [STFT](#id4) phases of the
microphone signals and not the respective magnitudes. The DDNN,
consequently, is biased towards speech sources if trained with speech or
towards spectrally white sources when trained with spectrally white
noise. In comparison, signal-processing methods for [DOA](#id1)
estimation do not exhibit such a bias towards spectral source
characteristics.

In the so-called sound event localization and detection (SELD) task
\[[29](#bib.bib29), [41](#bib.bib41), [43](#bib.bib43)\], the ability of
[DNN](#id6)s to be tailored to specific (spectral) source
characteristics for [DOA](#id1) estimation is exploited to localize
specific sources and their activity, only. In SELD, a [DNN](#id6) is
used to detect a sound event and the respective [DOA](#id1). In
\[[29](#bib.bib29), [41](#bib.bib41), [43](#bib.bib43)\], the
sources-of-interest have to be defined during training the DDNN. For
each [SOI](#id5) class, the DDNN has outputs for the respective source
activity and the [DOA](#id1). This approach requires retraining the DDNN
if the [SOI](#id5) changes. Additionally, the number of DDNN outputs has
to be increased each time the number of [SOI](#id5) classes increases,
which could introduce scaling problems for a high number of [SOI](#id5)
classes, or changing classes. An example of many changing classes is the
localization of multiple speakers, where each class represents a
specific speaker. In \[[29](#bib.bib29), [41](#bib.bib41),
[43](#bib.bib43)\], each [SOI](#id5) speaker had to be defined during
training and treated as an individual class on the DDNN output. Changing
[SOI](#id5) speakers would require retraining the DDNN, which is
impractical for many applications.

In SELD, a single [DNN](#id6) is designed to detect the activity of
sources-of-interest and determine their [DOA](#id1)s. Alternatively,
these two tasks can be separated via the concept of attention
\[[44](#bib.bib44), [46](#bib.bib46), [47](#bib.bib47),
[48](#bib.bib48), [54](#bib.bib54), [55](#bib.bib55), [46](#bib.bib46),
[56](#bib.bib56)\]. Systems using attention for [DOA](#id1) estimation
often consist of a [DOA](#id1) module, which estimates the [DOA](#id1)
(e.g., a DDNN or a signal-processing method) and an attention module,
which provides the attention that is used in the [DOA](#id1) module to
focus on the [SOI](#id5) and disregard interference, reverberation, and
noise. If the [SOI](#id5) selection is performed independently of the
[DOA](#id1) module (e.g., if the [DOA](#id1) module is a
signal-processing method), no [DOA](#id1) module change (architecture
change, retraining) is required for a changing or an increasing number
of [SOI](#id5) classes as in SELD \[[29](#bib.bib29), [41](#bib.bib41),
[43](#bib.bib43)\]. Only the attention has to be modified. Attention can
be estimated from spectral \[[44](#bib.bib44), [46](#bib.bib46),
[47](#bib.bib47), [48](#bib.bib48)\] or spatial \[[57](#bib.bib57)\]
features and can be implemented as a weighting applied to a feature
representation of the microphone signals in or before the [DOA](#id1)
module. The weighting concept of attention is similar to the
time-frequency masking concept for single-channel source
extraction/separation/enhancement (e.g., \[[58](#bib.bib58),
[59](#bib.bib59), [60](#bib.bib60), [61](#bib.bib61), [62](#bib.bib62),
[63](#bib.bib63), [64](#bib.bib64), [65](#bib.bib65), [66](#bib.bib66),
[67](#bib.bib67)\]), which allows adopting the concepts of this highly
investigated field to compute attention to enable signal-aware
[DOA](#id1) estimation. For example, a promising direction is to adopt
techniques from universal sound source separation for attention-based
multi-source [DOA](#id1) estimation \[[68](#bib.bib68),
[69](#bib.bib69)\]. Consequently, attention provides additional
flexibility.

Typically, the attention module is implemented in the form of a
[DNN](#id6) (referred to as ADNN) for both fully [DNN](#id6)-based
systems and hybrid systems, where a signal-processing method is used as
[DOA](#id1) module. In hybrid systems \[[54](#bib.bib54),
[55](#bib.bib55), [46](#bib.bib46), [56](#bib.bib56)\], the ADNN
estimates a time-frequency mask and was optimized using the ideal binary
mask \[[56](#bib.bib56), [46](#bib.bib46)\], the Wiener filter
\[[55](#bib.bib55)\], or the phase-sensitive mask \[[54](#bib.bib54)\]
as the target. That way, feature representations of the input signals
are modified to be dominated by the [SOI](#id5). Subsequently, MUSIC
\[[56](#bib.bib56)\], SRP-P \[[54](#bib.bib54), [55](#bib.bib55)\], or a
complex Watson mixture model \[[46](#bib.bib46)\] were used to estimate
the [DOA](#id1) of the [SOI](#id5). The [SOI](#id5), thereby, was
exclusively defined as a speech source. In \[[46](#bib.bib46)\], a
multi-speaker environment was considered where the [SOI](#id5) was
defined in a speakerbeam \[[70](#bib.bib70)\] like manner using a
reference audio snippet of the respective [SOI](#id5) (speaker)
processed in the ADNN. In \[[54](#bib.bib54), [55](#bib.bib55),
[56](#bib.bib56)\], the environment consisted of a single speech source
(the [SOI](#id5)) and non-speech interference or babble noise.

In fully [DNN](#id6)-based systems \[[48](#bib.bib48), [44](#bib.bib44),
[47](#bib.bib47)\], the ADNN estimates attention for a DDNN to enable
signal-aware [DOA](#id1) estimation. The DDNNs typically consist of a
[CNN](#id7) ([CNN](#id7)) to extract features from the microphone
signals and a subsequent [FFNN](#id9) ([FFNN](#id9)) to map the features
to the [DOA](#id1). Attention has been applied either before
\[[48](#bib.bib48), [47](#bib.bib47), [44](#bib.bib44)\] or after the
feature extracting [CNN](#id7) \[[48](#bib.bib48), [57](#bib.bib57)\].
In our preliminary work \[[48](#bib.bib48)\], we showed that attention
application after the [CNN](#id7) outperforms attention application at
the input. Training the ADNN has been done using masking-based
\[[47](#bib.bib47), [48](#bib.bib48), [44](#bib.bib44)\] or [E2E](#id3)
([E2E](#id3)) using [DOA](#id1)-based \[[44](#bib.bib44)\] objectives.
For low-SNR scenarios and unmatched training-test conditions,
[E2E](#id3) training performed best, whereas, for high SNR scenarios,
attention degraded the performance slightly compared to the
attention-free scenario \[[44](#bib.bib44)\]. As for the hybrid systems,
the focus of the fully [DNN](#id6)-based methods is on localizing speech
sources. In \[[47](#bib.bib47)\], the [SOI](#id5) is a specific speaker
defined by a spoken keyword in a multi-speaker environment, whereas in
\[[48](#bib.bib48), [44](#bib.bib44)\], there is only a single speaker
and non-speech interference.

To this point, it is not clear how hybrid systems perform in comparison
to fully [DNN](#id6)-based systems, although hybrid systems typically
exhibit a far lower computational complexity. Additionally, the effect
of attention on DDNNs is not yet investigated thoroughly. To investigate
the effect of attention on DDNNs, we evaluate different DDNN
architectures, input features, attention-application methods, and
training data simulation methods and compare their performance on data
simulated using measured room impulse responses (RIRs). In particular,
we investigate the importance of spectral context for DDNNs (see
Sections [3.1.3](#S3.SS1.SSS3 "3.1.3 Narrowband DDNNs ‣ 3.1 Modules ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
[3.2.2](#S3.SS2.SSS2 "3.2.2 End-to-End Training for Narrowband Estimators ‣ 3.2 Attention Module and Training Strategies ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Impact of Binary Frequency Selection on Estimation ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")),
whether DDNNs are biased towards a specific attention distribution via
training (see
Section [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Impact of Binary Frequency Selection on Estimation ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))
and whether the DDNN architecture can be reduced significantly dependent
on the input features/architecture (see
Sections [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Modules ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Impact of Binary Frequency Selection on Estimation ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")).
Subsequently, we evaluate different attention-application and DDNN/ADNN
training methods in
Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Impact of Training Data and Attention Application on Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms").
Finally, the best performing fully [DNN](#id6)-based system is compared
to different hybrid systems for signal-aware [DOA](#id1) estimation of a
single speech source in the presence of directional interference and
noise. Experiments with a fine-grained [DOA](#id1) resolution
($`\approx 1^{\circ}`$) and using measured data are conducted in
Section [5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Evaluation of Off-Grid s ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")
and
Section [5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Outlook: Evaluation using Measured Data of Moving Sources ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
respectively.

The main contributions can be summarized as follows: (I) Exhaustive
evaluation and comparison of existing and proposed methods for
signal-aware [DOA](#id1) estimation using simulated and measured data in
Section [5](#S5 "5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms").
(II) The proposition of novel training methods for fully
[DNN](#id6)-based and hybrid systems in
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Attention Module and Training Strategies ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms").
In particular, we propose: a) An [E2E](#id3) training method when
attention is applied in the DDNN - differences to \[[44](#bib.bib44)\]
are explained in
Section [2.2.2](#S2.SS2.SSS2 "2.2.2 Attention Application ‣ 2.2 Fully -Based Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")
and to \[[57](#bib.bib57)\] in
Section [3.2.1](#S3.SS2.SSS1 "3.2.1 End-to-End Training With Feature or Phase Masking ‣ 3.2 Attention Module and Training Strategies ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms");
b) A narrowband DDNN; c) Training an ADNN in combination with SRP-P with
a [DOA](#id1)-related loss (state-of-the-art is based on
masking/enhancement-related losses \[[54](#bib.bib54), [55](#bib.bib55),
[46](#bib.bib46), [56](#bib.bib56)\]) (III) Evaluation of the role of
attention and spectral context for DDNNs. The work presented here builds
upon our work \[[48](#bib.bib48)\] presented at ICASSP 2020.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In
Section [2](#S2 "2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
we introduce a signal model and introduce our preliminary work
\[[48](#bib.bib48)\] and baselines for hybrid \[[54](#bib.bib54)\] and
fully [DNN](#id6)-based \[[44](#bib.bib44)\] signal-aware [DOA](#id1)
estimation. Subsequently, we introduce the proposed modifications to the
[DNN](#id6) architecture from \[[48](#bib.bib48)\] and the proposed
training methods for hybrid and fully [DNN](#id6)-based systems. In
Section [4](#S4 "4 Data Sets ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
we describe the data sets used for evaluation and training. Finally, in
Section [5](#S5 "5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
we evaluate the proposed and baseline systems using measured and
simulated data.

## 2 Fundamentals

### 2.1 Problem Formulation

Figure 1: Scheme for [DOA](#id1) ($`\theta_{i}`$) estimation of the
$`i`$-th source.

We assume a uniform-linear microphone array (ULA) with $`Q`$ microphones
with microphone index $`q\in\{1,\ldots,Q\}`$ positioned in a reverberant
room with several directional sound sources. We define the microphone
signals in the [STFT](#id4) domain as
$`Y\in\mathbb{C}^{Q\times K\times N}`$, where $`\mathbb{C}`$ specifies
the complex domain, $`K`$ specifies the number of frequencies of the
one-sided [STFT](#id4) spectrum with frequency-index $`k\in\{1,...,K\}`$
and $`N`$ specifies the number of time-frames with time-frame index
$`n\in\{1,...,N\}`$. The microphone signals can be modelled as a
superposition of representations of the source signals
$`X_{i}\in\mathbb{C}^{Q\times K\times N}`$ with source index $`i`$ and
spatio-temporally white microphone self-noise
$`V\in\mathbb{C}^{Q\times K\times N}`$, i.e.,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       Y=\sum_{i=1}^{I}X_{i}+V,
       ```                       |     | (1) |

where $`I\in\mathbb{N}`$ is the number of sources. The source $`X_{i}`$
can be split into a direct component
$`X_{i}^{\textrm{d}}\in\mathbb{C}^{Q\times K\times N}`$ that reaches the
microphones without being reflected (e.g., from walls, or other
obstacles) and a reverberant component
$`X_{i}^{\textrm{r}}\in\mathbb{C}^{Q\times K\times N}`$, i.e.,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       X_{i}=X_{i}^{\textrm{d}}+X_{i}^{\textrm{r}}.
       ```                                           |     | (2) |

For a ULA, the [DOA](#id1) of the $`i`$-th source is defined as the
angle $`\theta_{i}\in[0,180]`$ which specifies the direction of the
$`i`$-th source to the microphone array as shown in
Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Problem Formulation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms").
From
Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Problem Formulation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
it can be inferred that this information is embedded in
$`X_{i}^{\textrm{d}}`$. Other sources, reverberation, or noise,
consequently complicate the [DOA](#id1) estimation of the $`i`$-th
source.

In a typical [DOA](#id1) estimation context, the objective is to
estimate from $`Y`$ the [DOA](#id1) of all $`I`$ sources. In
signal-aware [DOA](#id1) estimation, the aim is to estimate from $`Y`$
only the [DOA](#id1)s of the sources-of-interest, which are in a subset
of all $`I`$ sources. The definition of sources-of-interest, thereby, is
user and application-defined. To reduce the impact of reverberation,
noise, and interference on the [DOA](#id1) estimate and enable
signal-aware [DOA](#id1) estimation, attention in the form of a
weighting mask $`M\in[0,1]^{K\times N}`$ can be applied to $`Y`$ or a
feature representation of it. In [STFT](#id4) domain, the smallest unit
to estimate the [DOA](#id1) from is a single [STFT](#id4)-bin
$`Y[:,k,n]`$. The largest unit is the whole signal $`Y[:,:,:]`$. Strong
interference or pauses of the [SOI](#id5) can deteriorate to the final
[DOA](#id1) estimate. Via weighting with $`M`$, the influence of
[STFT](#id4)-bins that degrade the [DOA](#id1) estimation performance of
the sources-of-interest can be reduced.

If $`M`$ attends to multiple directional sound sources, there is no
assignment of the estimated [DOA](#id1)s to the respective
sources-of-interest. For multiple sources-of-interest, the weighting
$`M`$ can be constructed such that all sources-of-interest are attended
to simultaneously. Alternatively, different sound classes can be
defined, where each class, for example, represents a single speaker or a
collection of directional sounds. In this case, a weighting $`M_{u}`$
can be constructed to attend to a source belonging to the $`u`$-th
class. This process can be repeated for all sources-of-interest to
estimate their respective [DOA](#id1)s. For example, consider two active
sources-of-interest, a speaker and a loudspeaker playing music. When
both sources are attended to simultaneously with a single mask, two
[DOA](#id1)s are obtained without an assignment to speech and music.
With $`M_{1}`$ and $`M_{2}`$, each time one [DOA](#id1) is obtained,
where the assignment of $`M_{1}`$ and $`M_{2}`$ to speech and music,
respectively, allows assigning the respective [DOA](#id1)s to speech and
music in the same way. This has the additional advantage that two
[DOA](#id1)s are obtained even if the sources come from the same
direction. Using multiple masks enables multi-source [DOA](#id1)
estimation via single-source [DOA](#id1) estimation. Consequently, we
restrict the experiments to a single [SOI](#id5) of type speech without
loss of generality.

### 2.2 Fully [DNN](#id6)-Based Signal-Aware [DOA](#id1) Estimation

Figure 2: Scheme of the [DNN](#id6) system from our preliminary work
\[[48](#bib.bib48)\]. $`|\bullet|`$ symbolizes magnitude extraction of
the input and $`\angle\bullet`$ phase extraction of the respective
input. A DDNN based on a [CNN](#id7) and a [FFNN](#id9) maps the
[STFT](#id4) phases frame-wise to 37 [DOA](#id1) classes. Attention is
included in a) via feature masking \[see
([7](#S2.E7 "In 2.2.2 Attention Application ‣ 2.2 Fully -Based Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))\]
and alternatively in b) via phase masking \[see
([6](#S2.E6 "In 2.2.2 Attention Application ‣ 2.2 Fully -Based Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))\]
such that only the [SOI](#id5), here a speech source, is localized. The
attention is computed from the magnitude spectrum of one microphone
using a long short-term memory neural network (LSTM), the ADNN.

In this section, we review our recently proposed [DNN](#id6) for
signal-aware [DOA](#id1) estimation \[[48](#bib.bib48)\]. The
architecture is depicted in
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2.2 Fully -Based Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms").

#### 2.2.1 Architecture and Training

The DDNN \[[45](#bib.bib45)\] consists of two parts, a [CNN](#id7) and a
[FFNN](#id9). The [CNN](#id7) consists of $`Q-1`$ convolutional layers
with $`64`$ filters of shape $`(2,1)`$ (inter-microphone application),
each, stride $`1`$, padding $`0`$, and ReLU activation after each layer.
The [FFNN](#id9) consists of 3 layers with ReLU activation and a sigmoid
output activation with shapes $`(257\cdot 64,512)`$, $`(512,512)`$,
$`(512,C)`$, where $`C`$ represents a discrete representation of the
[DOA](#id1) space corresponding to angles
$`\widetilde{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{C}`$, where here $`C=37`$, and
$`\widetilde{\theta}[c]=(c-1)\cdot\frac{180}{C-1}^{\circ}`$, with
$`c\in\{1,\ldots,C\}`$. We denote the discrete [DOA](#id1)
representation for $`N`$ consecutive time-frames as
$`E\in[0,1]^{C\times N}`$. The input of the DDNN consists of the
microphone phases of a single time-frame $`n`$,
$`P[:,:,n]\in[-\pi,\pi]^{Q\times K}`$. We denote the features after the
[CNN](#id7) for $`N`$ separately processed time-frames as
$`F\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times 64\times N}`$, where 64 is the total number of
[CNN](#id7) filters, and $`N`$ specifies the number of processed
time-frames. Consequently, the [CNN](#id7) filters extract
inter-microphone but not inter-frequency information from $`P[:,:,n]`$.
Finally, the [FFNN](#id9) maps $`F[:,:,n]`$ to $`E[:,n]`$, where values
close to $`1`$ specify source activity in the respective direction in
time-frame $`n`$ \[[45](#bib.bib45)\], and zero specifies no activity.
The DDNN is trained with the [CCE](#id2) ([CCE](#id2)) loss on a
time-frame basis. Training data was simulated with noise and simulated
RIRs as in \[[38](#bib.bib38)\].

For evaluation, the time-frame estimates in $`E`$ can be combined by
averaging, i.e.,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \bar{E}[c]=\frac{1}{N}\cdot\sum_{n=1}^{N}E[c,n]\in[0,1],
       ```                                                       |     | (3) |

to obtain a global estimate. The estimated [DOA](#id1) of the
[SOI](#id5) is $`\widetilde{\theta}[\textrm{argmax}\{\bar{E}\}]`$ where
“argmax” returns the index of the maximum.

The ADNN maps the magnitude representation of a single microphone
$`|Y[1,:,:]|`$ to a ratio mask $`M_{r}\in[0,1]^{K\times N}`$ of equal
size for the speech source. The ADNN consist of a bidirectional long
short-term memory neural network (BLSTM) \[[71](#bib.bib71)\] with 3
layers and $`1200`$ neurons per layer. The output layer is a
feed-forward layer with sigmoid activation. The ADNN is trained for a
single-channel speech enhancement objective, to minimize the
mean-squared error (MSE) between the direct signal of the [SOI](#id5)
and the respective estimate at the first microphone,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{K\cdot N}\cdot\sum_{n}\sum_{k}(|X^{\textrm{d}}_{1}[1,k,n]|-|M_{r}[k,n]\cdot Y[1,k,n]|)^{2},
``` |  | (4) |

where only Source 1 is a speech source and all other sources are
non-speech.

#### 2.2.2 Attention Application

In \[[48](#bib.bib48)\], we proposed to compute binary attention
$`M_{b}[k,n]`$ for the speech source via thresholding, i.e.,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
M_{\text{b}}[k,n]=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }M_{\text{r}}[k,n]<v_{\text{thr}};\\
1&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}
``` |  | (5) |

where the threshold $`v_{\text{thr}}\in[0,1]`$. Subsequently,
$`M_{\text{b}}`$ can be applied to the DDNN via two methods. First, via
binary phase-masking (B-PM) by directly modifying the DDNN input $`P`$,
such that

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widetilde{P}[q,k,n]=M_{\text{b}}[k,n]\cdot P[q,k,n]+(1-M_{\text{b}}[k,n])\cdot\nu[q,k,n],
``` |  | (6) |

where $`\nu[q,k,n]\in[-\pi,\pi]`$ is a uniformly distributed random
variable and $`\widetilde{P}[:,:,n]`$ is the new DDNN input. Note that
$`\nu[q,k,n]`$ is used to avoid all-zero phase inputs in a frequency
band as this would correspond to a [DOA](#id1) of $`90^{\circ}`$. For
robust [DOA](#id1) estimation of a single source in the presence of
reverberation and noise, the authors in \[[44](#bib.bib44)\] proposed a
similar phase masking approach as in
([6](#S2.E6 "In 2.2.2 Attention Application ‣ 2.2 Fully -Based Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")),
with $`v_{q}=0`$ and ratio attention $`M_{\text{r}}[k,n]\in[0,1]`$
instead of $`M_{\text{b}}[k,n]`$. We refer to phase masking with
$`M_{\text{r}}`$ and $`v_{q}=0`$ using our [DNN](#id6) architecture as
ratio phase-masking without randomization (referred to as R-PM\*) and
compare it to B-PM and ratio phase-masking with randomization, which is
described in
Section [3.2.1](#S3.SS2.SSS1 "3.2.1 End-to-End Training With Feature or Phase Masking ‣ 3.2 Attention Module and Training Strategies ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms").

Secondly, attention can be applied via binary feature-masking (B-FM) by
zeroing selected features after the [CNN](#id7), i.e.,

|     |                                                       |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \widetilde{F}[k,:,n]=F[k,:,n]\cdot M_{\text{b}}[k,n],
       ```                                                    |     | (7) |

where $`F[:,:,n]`$ are the features after the [CNN](#id7), and
$`\widetilde{F}[:,:,n]`$ are masked features (see Figure 
[2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2.2 Fully -Based Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))
which are fed in the [FFNN](#id9) instead of $`F[:,:,n]`$ when B-FM is
used. The same binary attention value, thereby, is used for all 64
features in a specific time-frequency bin. Please note that either B-PM
or B-FM is applied in previous works and that an application of both
would be equal to B-FM \[[48](#bib.bib48)\].

### 2.3 Baseline System: Hybrid Signal-Aware [DOA](#id1) Estimation

In \[[54](#bib.bib54), [55](#bib.bib55)\], the authors proposed a
steered-response power with modified PHAT weighting (SRP-MP) to perform
signal-aware [DOA](#id1) estimation. Attention, thereby, is used to
modify the PHAT weighting. In \[[55](#bib.bib55)\], attention is
computed from averaged microphone features using an ADNN trained for a
Wiener filter objective. In \[[54](#bib.bib54)\], attention is computed
from each microphone separately and is trained using a variant of the
phase-sensitive mask (PSM) for the speech source as the target, i.e.,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{PSM}[q,k,n]=\max\left\{0,\sqrt{\frac{|X^{\textrm{d}}_{1}[q,k,n]|^{2}}{|X^{\textrm{d}}_{1}[q,k,n]|^{2}+|Y[q,k,n]-X^{\textrm{d}}_{1}[q,k,n]|^{2}}}\cdot\cos(\angle X^{\textrm{d}}_{1}[q,k,n]-P[q,k,n])\right\},
``` |  | (8) |

where $`\angle X^{\textrm{d}}_{1}[q,k,n]`$ provides the phase of
$`X^{\textrm{d}}_{1}[q,k,n]`$. In SRP-P and SRP-MP, the microphone
signals are transformed in the [STFT](#id4) domain, and each
time-frequency bin is normalized with its magnitude (PHAT weighting).
The PHAT weighting can be denoted as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{W}[q,k,n]=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{|Y[q,k,n]|}&\text{if }|Y[q,k,n]|>\epsilon;\\
\epsilon&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}
``` |  | (9) |

with the small constant $`\epsilon\in\mathbb{R}^{+}`$. Subsequently, the
power of the normalized spectrum coming from different sampled
directions is computed. The [DOA](#id1) is obtained by picking the
direction with the maximum power.

For signal-aware [DOA](#id1) estimation, the PHAT weighting can be
modified by applying the mask $`M_{\text{r}}`$ to it, i.e.,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widetilde{\text{W}}[q,k,n]=\text{W}[q,k,n]\cdot M_{\text{r}}[k,n],
``` |  | (10) |

to obtain a new weighting function. In \[[55](#bib.bib55)\], the same
$`M_{\text{r}}`$ is used for all microphones, whereas in
\[[54](#bib.bib54)\], the mask is channel dependent. We refer to the
application of the SRP-P algorithm with weighting
$`\widetilde{\text{W}}`$ as SRP-MP¹¹ 1 Derivation of the equality of
PHAT weighting and
([9](#S2.E9 "In 2.3 Baseline System: Hybrid Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))
can be found in \[[15](#bib.bib15)\].. Subsequently, the weighting is
applied to the microphone signals and the matrix
$`\Phi\in\mathbb{C}^{K\times N\times Q\times Q}`$ is computed, i.e.,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Phi[k,n,q_{1},q_{2}]=Y[q_{1},k,n]\cdot\widetilde{\text{W}}[q_{1},k,n]\cdot\widetilde{\text{W}}[q_{2},k,n]\cdot Y^{*}[q_{2},k,n],
``` |  | (11) |

where ^(∗) denotes the complex conjugate. As in SRP-P
\[[15](#bib.bib15)\], the [DOA](#id1) space is sampled assuming a
far-field model and relative transfer functions
$`D\in\mathbb{C}^{C\times K\times Q}`$ w.r.t. the first microphone,
where a single element is denoted as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
D[c,k,q]=\mathrm{e}^{\frac{-j\cdot 2\cdot\pi\cdot k\cdot f_{s}\cdot\cos(\widetilde{\theta}[c])\cdot d_{q}}{c_{s}\cdot K}},
``` |  | (12) |

where $`\mathrm{e}`$ is Euler’s number, $`c_{s}`$ is the speed of sound,
$`f_{s}`$ is the sampling frequency, $`j=\sqrt{-1}`$ is the complex
unit, and $`d_{q}`$ denotes the distance between the first and the
$`q`$-th microphone. Finally, SRP-MP steered to all elements in
$`\widetilde{\theta}`$ is obtained via

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{SRP-MP}[c](\Phi)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathop{\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\sum_{j=q+1}^{Q}}\left(\frac{2\cdot\textrm{Real}\{\text{D}[c,k,q]\cdot\Phi[k,n,q,j]\cdot\text{D}^{*}[c,k,j]\}}{N\cdot K\cdot(Q-1)\cdot(Q-1)}\right),
``` |  | (13) |

where “Real” provides the real part, only. Finally,
$`\bar{E}_{\text{SRP-MP}}`$ is obtained by normalizing SRP-MP, i.e.,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{E}_{\text{SRP-MP}}[c]=\frac{\text{SRP-MP}[c]}{\text{max}_{1\leq u\leq C}(\text{SRP-MP}[u])}.
``` |  | (14) |

The same normalization procedure can be applied to SRP-P, which results
in $`\bar{E}_{\text{SRP-P}}`$. The estimated [DOA](#id1)
$`\widehat{\theta}`$ of the [SOI](#id5) is
$`\widetilde{\theta}[\textrm{argmax}\{\bar{E}\}]`$ where “argmax”
returns the index of the maximum. Note that the SRP-MP approach differs
from SRP-P \[[15](#bib.bib15)\] only in the application of
$`M_{\text{r}}`$ in
([10](#S2.E10 "In 2.3 Baseline System: Hybrid Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")),
which is not used in SRP-P.

As SRP-P is solely model-based (not data-driven) and the individual ADNN
input is from a single microphone \[[54](#bib.bib54)\], the ADNN of
SRP-MP can be trained once, and then it can be used for any (static or
dynamic) microphone architecture by adjusting the SRP-P model. Note that
$`M_{\text{r}}`$ can nevertheless be array dependent, and unmatched
array architectures during training and testing could lead to degraded
results compared to the matched scenario. In contrast, as DDNNs are
connected to a specific array architecture via training (e.g., fixed
inter-microphone distance, number of microphones, etc.), an application
to a different array cannot yield reasonable results. Consequently,
retraining is required, and sometimes even modifications to the DDNN
architecture are necessary due to a different number of microphones. For
implementation details of SRP-MP/SRP-P, we refer to \[[15](#bib.bib15),
[72](#bib.bib72)\].

We like to note that the computational complexity of SRP-MP is much
lower than of the [DNN](#id6)s. To assess computational complexity, we
follow the approach in \[[73](#bib.bib73)\] and count the number of
multiplications/divisions, additions/subtractions, i.e., the number of
[flops](#id12) ([flops](#id12)). Non-linearities are not taken into
account. A more accurate complexity analysis would require knowledge
about the employed hardware. Assuming complex numbers to be represented
by a real and imaginary part, SRP-P requires $`5\cdot K\cdot Q`$
real-valued divisions per time-frame to compute and apply the PHAT
weighting to each microphone. Efficiently implemented, SRP-P requires
$`6\cdot K\cdot\frac{(Q-1)^{2}}{2}`$ operations to compute the
upper-triangle components of
([11](#S2.E11 "In 2.3 Baseline System: Hybrid Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))
and approximately $`4\cdot K\cdot C\cdot\frac{(Q-1)^{2}}{2}`$ operations
to compute the components in
([13](#S2.E13 "In 2.3 Baseline System: Hybrid Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))
per time-frame. In total this sums up to approximately
$`\frac{(Q-1)^{2}}{2}\cdot(4\cdot K\cdot C+6\cdot K)+5\cdot K\cdot Q`$
[flops](#id12). For $`K=257`$, $`C=37`$ and $`Q=4`$ the number of
[flops](#id12) is lower than $`0.2\cdot 10^{6}`$. For comparison, see
the [flops](#id12) of the [DNN](#id6)s in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Modules ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms").

## 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective [DOA](#id1) Estimation

In this section, we propose different systems and training strategies
for signal-aware [DOA](#id1) estimation using attention. A system,
thereby, consists of a module for attention and another module for
[DOA](#id1) estimation. We compare these systems to
\[[48](#bib.bib48)\], \[[54](#bib.bib54)\], and the R-PM\* concept of
\[[44](#bib.bib44)\] in the performance evaluation.

### 3.1 [DOA](#id1) Modules

In the following, we describe the proposed extensions and modifications
of our preliminary work \[[48](#bib.bib48)\]. In
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Modules ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
we present various variants of different DDNNs designed to investigate
specific research questions. We modified the architecture from
\[[48](#bib.bib48)\] by including batch normalization layers
\[[74](#bib.bib74)\] between the [CNN](#id7)s as it is known to reduce
training time and makes the model less prone to the initialized weights.
These models are marked with a superscript B in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Modules ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms").

| \# | Abbreviation | Feature | BN | \# [CNN](#id7)s | Size [FFNN](#id9) | NB | \# FLOPS |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| 1 | $`\text{CNN}^{\tiny{B}}_{\tiny{\Delta P}}`$ | $`\Delta P`$ | ✓ | $`Q-2`$ | 64$`\cdot`$257;512;512;37 | ✗ | $`\approx 22\cdot 10^{6}`$ |
| 2 | $`\text{CNN}^{\tiny{N,B}}_{\tiny{\Delta P}}`$ | $`\Delta P`$ | ✓ | $`Q-2`$ | 64;74;74;37 | ✓ | $`\approx 11\cdot 10^{6}`$ |
| 3 | $`\text{CNN}_{\tiny{\Delta P}}`$ | $`\Delta P`$ | ✗ | $`Q-2`$ | 64$`\cdot`$257;512;512;37 | ✗ | $`\approx 22\cdot 10^{6}`$ |
| 4 | $`\text{CNN}^{\tiny{N}}_{\tiny{\Delta P}}`$ | $`\Delta P`$ | ✗ | $`Q-2`$ | 64;74;74;37 | ✓ | $`\approx 11\cdot 10^{6}`$ |
| 5 | $`\text{CNN}^{\tiny{B}}_{\tiny{P}}`$ | $`P`$ | ✓ | $`Q-1`$ | 64$`\cdot`$257;512;512;37 | ✗ | $`\approx 30\cdot 10^{6}`$ |
| 6 | $`\text{CNN}^{\tiny{N,B}}_{\tiny{P}}`$ | $`P`$ | ✓ | $`Q-1`$ | 64;74;74;37 | ✓ | $`\approx 19\cdot 10^{6}`$ |
| 7 | $`\text{CNN}_{\tiny{P}}`$ | $`P`$ | ✗ | $`Q-1`$ | 64$`\cdot`$257;512;512;37 | ✗ | $`\approx 30\cdot 10^{6}`$ |
| 8 | $`\text{CNN}^{\tiny{N}}_{\tiny{P}}`$ | $`P`$ | ✗ | $`Q-1`$ | 64;74;74;37 | ✓ | $`\approx 19\cdot 10^{6}`$ |
| 9 | $`\text{FFNN}_{\tiny{\Delta P}}`$ | $`\Delta P`$ | ✗ | 0 | ($`Q-1`$)$`\cdot`$257;512;512;37 | ✗ | $`\approx 1.4\cdot 10^{6}`$ |
| 10 | $`\text{FFNN}^{\tiny{N}}_{\tiny{\Delta P}}`$ | $`\Delta P`$ | ✗ | 0 | $`Q-1`$;74;74;37 | ✓ | $`\approx 4.3\cdot 10^{6}`$ |
| 11 | $`\text{FFNN}_{\tiny{P}}`$ | $`P`$ | ✗ | 0 | $`Q\cdot`$257;512;512;37 | ✗ | $`\approx 1.6\cdot 10^{6}`$ |
| 12 | $`\text{FFNN}^{\tiny{N}}_{\tiny{P}}`$ | $`P`$ | ✗ | 0 | $`Q`$;74;74;37 | ✓ | $`\approx 4.4\cdot 10^{6}`$ |

Table 1: Overview of all DDNNs: “Feature” specifies the input of the
DDNN. “BN” specifies whether additional 2D batch normalization layers
(size 64 = number of [CNN](#id7) filters per layer) are between the
[CNN](#id7) layers. “Size [FFNN](#id9)” specifies the sizes of the 3
feed-forward layers in the format:
input-l1;output-l1;output-l2;output-l3. For the narrowband models, the
size of the three feed-forward layers is given for each frequency band.
“NB” specifies whether there is an [FFNN](#id9) per frequency band
(narrowband) or a single [FFNN](#id9) processing all frequency bands
together to map $`F`$ to the [DOA](#id1). “Abbreviation” specifies the
abbreviation we use for the respective [DNN](#id6). The [CNN](#id7)s
have 64 filters of shape $`(2,1)`$, each, a stride of 1, no padding as
in \[[40](#bib.bib40)\]. We use a ReLU activation after each hidden
layer and a sigmoid activation after the output layer. Between each
feed-forward layer, we use a dropout of 0.5 as in \[[45](#bib.bib45)\].
The number of [flops](#id12) gives the approximate number of
multiplications and additions required by each of the models per
time-frame (without the masking network) for $`Q=4`$, $`K=257`$,
$`C=37`$.

#### 3.1.1 Phase Vs. Phase Difference Input

The [DOA](#id1) information is, according to physical models, given in
the inter-microphone phase-differences denoted as
$`\Delta P\in[-\pi,\pi]^{Q-1\times K\times N}`$, where
$`\Delta P[q,k,n]=\text{MOD}(P[q+1,k,n]-P[q,k,n],\pi)`$, where MOD is
the modulo operator. The information of the phase differences is in the
phases, however, with an additional random offset. Consequently, mapping
microphone phases to the [DOA](#id1) is a many-to-one mapping due to a
random phase offset on the microphone phase-differences. When using the
phase difference, a frequency-dependent one-to-one mapping exists (in
the absence of noise and other distortions) from the input features to
the DOA. In
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Modules ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
these [DNN](#id6)s are marked with a $`\Delta P`$ in the “Feature”
column. Note that using $`\Delta P`$ as input reduces the number of
[CNN](#id7) layers to $`Q-2`$.

#### 3.1.2 Parameter Reduction

The number of parameters of the DDNN \[[48](#bib.bib48)\] is dominated
by the weight matrix of the first feed-forward layer. The size of this
layer is very large due to the multiplication of the number of
[CNN](#id7) filters with the number of frequency bands (see
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Modules ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")).
If the [CNN](#id7) is removed, the number of frequency bands is only
multiplied with the number of microphones resulting in a parameter
reduction of approximately $`\frac{Q}{64}`$. Consequently, we propose a
DDNN without [CNN](#id7)s to investigate whether this massive parameter
reduction leads to performance degradation. In
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Modules ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
these [DNN](#id6)s are abbreviated with “FFNN”.

#### 3.1.3 Narrowband DDNNs

Figure 3: Narrowband DDNN with an independent [FFNN](#id9) per frequency
band.

Many signal processing-based [DOA](#id1) estimators perform narrowband
[DOA](#id1) estimation and subsequently merge the narrowband estimates
(e.g., via averaging \[[75](#bib.bib75)\]) to obtain a broadband
estimate. Motivated by these approaches, we propose to use the same
rationale for [DOA](#id1) estimation with a [DNN](#id6). We assume such
a procedure has an additional advantage in the case of signal-aware
[DOA](#id1) estimation, where some frequency bands have to be
disregarded. In \[[48](#bib.bib48)\], this was achieved using binary
masking (B-PM, B-FM). The band selection, thereby, strongly depends on
the spectral characteristics of the interference and the desired
signals. Both B-PM and B-FM may introduce different kinds of noise,
dependent on the spectral characteristics of the sources, in the
[DOA](#id1) estimation as the zeroed/randomized features are fed in the
DDNN. Suppose the [DOA](#id1) is estimated independently per frequency
band. In that case, the [DOA](#id1) estimates of the individual bands
can subsequently be combined (e.g., by averaging the [DOA](#id1)
estimates over the frequency) to obtain a broadband estimate.
Additionally, we hypothesize that such a process is more robust w.r.t.
masking than B-FM and B-PM as zeroed/randomized inputs are not fed in
the DDNN. As the [CNN](#id7) filters only combine inter-microphone but
not inter-frequency information, it is sufficient to modify the DDNN in
\[[48](#bib.bib48)\] such that there is an individual [FFNN](#id9) with
sigmoid output activation per frequency band. A scheme of this
architecture is given in
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1.3 Narrowband DDNNs ‣ 3.1 Modules ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms").
In
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Modules ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
these [DNN](#id6)s are marked with a ✓in the “NB” column.

### 3.2 Attention Module and Training Strategies

For comparability, we use the same ADNN architecture for all [DOA](#id1)
modules (proposed and baselines). The ADNN consists of 2 long short-term
memory layers (LSTM) (input dim. = 257, hidden dim. = 512) followed by a
feed-forward layer with an output shape of 257 with sigmoid activation.
Per time-frame, this model requires approximately $`7.6`$ million
[flops](#id12)²² 2 [flops](#id12) of feed-forward layers are computed by
doubling the multiplication of the input dimension with the output
dimension to account for multiplications and additions. An LSTM layer
contains 4 feed-forward matrices of shape (input dim.$`\times`$ hidden
dim.), and 4 feed-forward matrices of shape (hidden dim.$`\times`$
hidden dim.). [flops](#id12) of CNN layers are computed by doubling the
multiplication of the output dimension with the filter dimension, and
the number of filters. Non-linearities or batch-normalization layers are
not taken into account.. The input/output shapes are selected such that
they fit the number of frequency bins per [STFT](#id4) time-frame of the
input. In contrast to \[[48](#bib.bib48)\], we use an LSTM with fewer
parameters instead of a BLSTM to enable online [DOA](#id1) estimation.
We used a dropout of 0.4 between the LSTM layers and of 0.7 before the
output layer during training to avoid overfitting \[[76](#bib.bib76)\].
In \[[48](#bib.bib48)\], we optimized the ADNN using a speech
enhancement objective. In particular, we selected frequency bands in a
binary fashion to estimate the [DOA](#id1). This binary selection breaks
the gradient path, as the rounding to either 0 or 1 is
non-differentiable. Consequently, the ADNN cannot be trained [E2E](#id3)
with the [DOA](#id1) estimation objective using supervised learning.
Additionally, to train the ADNN [E2E](#id3), training data cannot be
simulated using noise as in \[[38](#bib.bib38), [40](#bib.bib40)\] as
the ADNN has to learn the spectral and temporal characteristics of the
[SOI](#id5). Consequently, training data must be simulated with the
[SOI](#id5). Using the time-frame-based training method in
\[[38](#bib.bib38), [40](#bib.bib40)\] would require an activity
detection for the [SOI](#id5). To avoid [SOI](#id5) activity detection
and train the ADNN and the DDNN [E2E](#id3), we propose different
training strategies using ratio instead of binary attention techniques
for frequency bin selection.

#### 3.2.1 End-to-End Training With Feature or Phase Masking

The ADNNs yield the (single-channel) ratio attention
$`M_{\text{r}}\in[0,1]^{K\times N}`$ for $`N`$ successive time-frames.
We assume the source to be static, i.e., it does not move for $`N`$
time-frames. We propose to apply $`M_{\text{r}}`$ \[rather than
$`M_{\text{b}}`$ as in
([6](#S2.E6 "In 2.2.2 Attention Application ‣ 2.2 Fully -Based Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))
and
([7](#S2.E7 "In 2.2.2 Attention Application ‣ 2.2 Fully -Based Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))\]
to the features, i.e.,

|     |                                                       |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \widetilde{F}[k,:,n]=F[k,:,n]\cdot M_{\text{r}}[k,n],
       ```                                                    |     | (15) |

or to the input, i.e.,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widetilde{P}[q,k,n]=M_{\text{r}}[k,n]\cdot P[q,k,n]+(1-M_{\text{r}}[k,n])\cdot\nu[q,k,n].
``` |  | (16) |

We refer to the application of ratio attention in
([15](#S3.E15 "In 3.2.1 End-to-End Training With Feature or Phase Masking ‣ 3.2 Attention Module and Training Strategies ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))
and
([16](#S3.E16 "In 3.2.1 End-to-End Training With Feature or Phase Masking ‣ 3.2 Attention Module and Training Strategies ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))
as ratio feature-masking (R-FM) and ratio phase-masking (R-PM),
respectively. The respective DDNN output is marked as $`E_{\text{FM}}`$,
or $`E_{\text{PM}}`$. For evaluation over multiple time-frames it is
common \[[45](#bib.bib45)\] to gather [DOA](#id1) information across
consecutive time-frames by averaging, i.e.,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{E}_{\bullet}[e]=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}E_{\bullet}[:,n]\in[0,1]^{37},
``` |  | (17) |

where $`\bullet`$ specifies either FM or PM. We propose to use the same
averaging concept for training. Using several time-frames for training
enables training without the necessity for a source activity detector
(e.g., see \[[77](#bib.bib77)\]) as the [DOA](#id1)s of silent
time-frames average out and allow the LSTM of the ADNN to exploit
temporal context for attention estimation. Note that the [DOA](#id1)
label is only based on the [DOA](#id1) of the [SOI](#id5) but not on the
other interfering sources. Please note, in contrast to
\[[48](#bib.bib48)\], $`M_{\text{r}}`$ provides a soft rather than
binary attention. We investigate training the ADNN and the DDNN together
using the [CCE](#id2) loss for a [DOA](#id1) objective. In the
performance evaluation, we investigate using a pre-trained DDNN with
noise \[[38](#bib.bib38)\]. Subsequently, the DDNN weights are frozen,
and the ADNN is trained [E2E](#id3) with the DDNN (frozen weights) for a
[DOA](#id1) estimation objective via the [CCE](#id2) loss. With these
experiments we investigate whether the DDNNs are biased via training
towards specific spectral source characteristics and attention
distributions.

In parallel to the present work, \[[57](#bib.bib57)\] proposed to use
feature masking trained end-to-end with an automatic speech recognition
loss. In particular, the authors proposed to average the [CNN](#id7)
features before the [FFNN](#id9) such that the [FFNN](#id9) learns to
map denoised features to the [DOA](#id1). To avoid bias of the
[FFNN](#id9), we propose to average the frame-wise [DOA](#id1) estimates
after the [FFNN](#id9) for training purposes only. In that way, the DDNN
still operates on a time-frame basis. Additionally, in
\[[57](#bib.bib57)\], the authors estimate attention from the spatial
features obtained by the CNN of the STFT phases (i.e., without using the
magnitude information); In contrast, we estimate attention from the
magnitude STFT to differentiate between the SOI and other sound sources.

#### 3.2.2 End-to-End Training for Narrowband Estimators

For the narrowband DDNNs, R-PM or R-FM is not necessary, as we obtain a
separate [DOA](#id1) per frequency band, denoted as
$`E_{\text{NB}}\in[0,1]^{37\times K\times N}`$. Consequently, we propose
to weight the individual estimates to obtain a single broadband
estimate, i.e.,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{E}_{\text{NB}}[c]=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{n=1}^{N}M_{\text{r}}[k,n]\cdot E_{\text{NB}}[c,k,n]}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{n=1}^{N}M_{\text{r}}[k,n]}.
``` |  | (18) |

We refer to this weighting using a ratio mask as output masking
($`\text{OM}_{r}`$). We use the [CCE](#id2) loss between the label and
$`\bar{E}_{\text{NB}}`$ for training.

#### 3.2.3 DOA-Based Training using SRP-MP

Finally, we compare the DDNN based approaches with SRP-MP. To train the
ADNN using a [DOA](#id1) objective, we propose to minimize the MSE
between the SRP-P [SPS](#id10) ([SPS](#id10)) obtained from the clean
non-reverberant signals $`X^{\textrm{d}}_{1}`$ (denoted as
$`\bar{E}^{X_{1}^{\textrm{d}}}_{\textrm{SRP-P}}`$) and the SRP-MP
[SPS](#id10) obtained from the mixture signals $`Y`$, i.e.,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
J_{\textrm{SRP-MP}}=\frac{1}{C}\sum_{c}\left(\bar{E}_{\textrm{SRP-MP}}[c]-\bar{E}^{X_{1}^{\textrm{d}}}_{\textrm{SRP-P}}[c]\right)^{2}.
``` |  | (19) |

We implemented the SRP-P code \[[72](#bib.bib72)\] in PyTorch to enable
training and included the attention mechanism. Note that a [CCE](#id2)
loss cannot be applied here, as even the SRP-P estimate of the
non-reverberant, noise, and interference-free signals exhibit broad
lobes with non-zero entries aside from the desired [DOA](#id1).
Consequently, these non-zero entries cannot be removed in the proposed
framework such that the [CCE](#id2) loss cannot be applied.

## 4 Data Sets

|  | Training | Validation | Test Measured \[[78](#bib.bib78)\] | Test Simulated |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| $`T_{60}[s]`$ | {$`.2,.3,.4,.6,.8`$} | {$`.45,.6,.75`$} | {$`.16,.36,.61`$} | {$`.38,.7`$} |
| SMD \[m\] | $`\{1,2\}`$ | $`\{1.2,2.3\}`$ | $`\{1,2\}`$ | $`\{1.3,1.7\}`$ |
| $`\theta\>[^{\circ}]`$ | $`\{0,5,\ldots,180\}`$ | $`\{0,5,\ldots,180\}`$ | $`\{0,15,\ldots,180\}`$ | $`\{0,\frac{180}{179},\ldots,180\}`$ |

Table 2: Parameters of the RIRs for the different data sets.

The data sets used for training, validation, and test are introduced in
this section. The [STFT](#id4) parameters were a sampling frequency of
$`16`$ kHz, a hop-size of $`16`$ ms, and a window-length of $`32`$ ms
such that $`K=257`$. Each file contains speech at its center. Parts
($`N=100`$) of longer speech files were extracted based on local energy
accumulations around the center to exclude silent files/files with
little speech activity. Subsequently, the files are convolved with RIRs
and cut to $`N=100`$ ($`\approx 1.6`$ s).

### 4.1 Room Impulse Responses

For training, validation, and test, different RIRs were simulated using
the image-method \[[79](#bib.bib79), [80](#bib.bib80)\]. For test, also
measured RIRs were used from \[[78](#bib.bib78)\]. All RIRs specify a
ULA with four microphones and an 8 cm inter-microphone distance. From
\[[78](#bib.bib78)\], we used the central four microphones from the
eight microphones 8 cm configuration. The RIR parameters, like the
source microphone-center distance (SMD) or the reverberation time
$`T_{60}`$, are summarized in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4 Data Sets ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms").
The training, validation, and test RIRs were simulated in different
rooms $`[m]`$,
$`\{[6,6,2.7],[5,4,2.7],[10,6,2.7],[8,3,2.7],[8,5,2.7]\}`$ for training,
and $`\{[9,11,2.7],[10,10,2.7],[9,5,2.7]\}`$ for validation, and
$`\{[9,4,3],[5,7,3]\}`$ for the simulated test set (testSIMRIR). Note
that although the SMD in training and the measured test (testMEASRIR) is
the same, the different reverberation times and rooms change the
direct-to-reverberation ratio such that it can be seen as unmatched
conditions. testMEASRIR consists of
$`T_{60}\cdot\text{SMD}\cdot\text{\acs{DOA}s}=3\cdot 2\cdot 13=78`$ RIR
configurations \[RIRs to all microphones\]. Combining the rooms with the
parameters from
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4 Data Sets ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")
results in $`3\cdot 50\cdot 37`$, $`18\cdot 37`$, $`8\cdot 180`$ RIR
configurations for the training, validation, and simulated test sets,
where $`37`$ and $`180`$ are the numbers of [DOA](#id1)s, respectively.
For each simulation, the microphone array was placed randomly in the
room. The source was placed according to the respective ground-truth
[DOA](#id1) and SMD. The constellation was rotated randomly around a
random axis. The minimum distance from all microphones and the source to
the wall was set to 1 m. For the training RIRs, the generation process
was repeated three times.

### 4.2 Single-Source Data Sets

To investigate the influence of attention on the performance of DDNNs,
we generate data sets with a single speech source and spatiotemporally
white microphone self-noise with a signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR)
$`\in[10,30]`$ dB. Speech files from the test set from Librispeech
\[[81](#bib.bib81)\] were convolved with the RIRs from testMEASRIR. Per
microphone configuration, the process was repeated 20 times with a
random SNR. For the training and validation set, we generated data by
convolving the training and validation RIR sets with white noise as in
\[[38](#bib.bib38)\]. From each resulting file, we selected the first
$`1.6~s`$, which results in 100 [STFT](#id4) frames per file
($`\approx~1.6~s`$). The total number of training, validation, and test
time-frames is $`11.1\cdot 1e6`$, $`1.3\cdot 1e6`$, and $`156\cdot 1e3`$
[STFT](#id4) frames for the respective sets. We refer to these sets as
train-1S, val-1S, and test-1S.

### 4.3 Two-Sources Data Sets

To investigate the effect of [E2E](#id3) training for signal-aware
[DOA](#id1) estimation of the ADNN and the DDNN, we generate training,
validation, and test sets consisting of two sources
(signal-to-interference ratio (SIR) $`\in[-6,6]`$ dB) and
spatiotemporally white microphone self-noise with an SNR
$`\in[20,30]`$ dB. The first source is always a speech source from the
respective set of Librispeech \[[81](#bib.bib81)\]. The second source is
random interference, e.g., guitar, engine, piano, …, from the respective
sets of the YouTube-based FSDnoisy18k \[[82](#bib.bib82),
[83](#bib.bib83)\]. Due to the temporal sparsity of some files in
FSDnoisy18k, we computed local energy accumulations to select
energy-rich source segments such that very sparse files can be excluded.
Please note, the second source does not contain speech. The [DOA](#id1)
of the speech source is selected deterministically to yield a uniform
distribution over all $`C`$ possible [DOA](#id1)s. The [DOA](#id1) of
the interfering source was selected randomly from all $`C`$ [DOA](#id1)s
with a spatial separation of both sources larger than $`5^{\circ}`$ for
evaluation purposes. The rest of the procedure is similar to the
single-source case resulting in the same number of time-frames in the
respective sets. We refer to these sets as train-2S, val-2S, and
test-2S. Additionally, we generated a third high-resolution test set
referred to as test-2S-HR with the RIRs from testSIMRIR with a total of
$`\approx 2.88\cdot 1e6`$ [STFT](#id4) frames. Note that for this test
set, the minimum angular distance between both sources is larger than
$`\frac{180}{179}^{\circ}`$.

For training the ADNNs, we used the signals of the first microphone of
the training sets.

respective mask $`M_{\text{b}}`$ consists of ones in the 50 randomly
selected bands and zeros, elsewhere. In the fourth column, the frequency
bands 100 to 150 were used (dB-FM/dB-OM). Models 13 and 14 are DDNNs
trained for [DOA](#id1) estimation only (not signal-aware). Model 13 is
the DDNN basis we extended in \[[48](#bib.bib48)\] for signal-aware
[DOA](#id1) estimation. The trained weights of the Models 13 and 14 are
available on
https://github.com/Soumitro-Chakrabarty/Single-speaker-localization.
Model 15 and 16 are standard implementations of MUSIC and SRP-P from the
pyroomacoustics library \[[72](#bib.bib72)\] that were evaluated on the
randomly/deterministically selected frequency bands. In MUSIC, we
additionally used the band-wise normalization proposed in
\[[75](#bib.bib75)\]. “No Masking” is equivalent to a mask that consists
of ones, only. The results in the table demonstrate the effect of
attention on [DOA](#id1) estimators.

We evaluate the ADNNS and DDNNs using the mean absolute error (MAE),
accuracy (ACC), and pseudo accuracy (psACC) metrics. The MAE is the
average over several files of the [AE](#id11) ([AE](#id11)), which is
defined as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{AE}=\left|\theta_{1}-\widetilde{\theta}\left[\textrm{argmax}\left\{\sum_{n=1}^{N_{\textrm{e}}}E_{\bullet}[n,:]\right\}\right]\right|,
``` |  | (20) |

where $`N_{\textrm{e}}`$ is the considered number of time-frames per
file for evaluation in the test set. We assume a result to be accurate
if the AE is smaller than $`5^{\circ}`$ and pseudo accurate if the AE is
smaller than $`10^{\circ}`$ such that the neighbouring classes of the
DDNN output are included. We report these metrics on a frame
($`N_{\textrm{e}}=1`$), a 50-frame ($`\approx 0.8~s`$,
$`N_{\textrm{e}}=50`$), or 100-frame ($`\approx 1.6~s`$,
$`N_{\textrm{e}}=100`$) basis to show the performance of the algorithms
over different context lengths. The desired length $`N_{\textrm{e}}`$,
thereby, depends on the application. For tracking fast moving sources,
for example, a small $`N_{\textrm{e}}`$ is required to provide
sufficient temporal resolution. For slowly moving or static sources, a
large $`N_{\textrm{e}}`$ might be beneficial to increase the [DOA](#id1)
estimation accuracy. As the focus of the paper is the localization of
static sources, we base most of our experiments on $`N_{\textrm{e}}=50`$
or $`N_{\textrm{e}}=100`$. Unless stated differently, all [DOA](#id1)
estimators (signal processing and [DNN](#id6)-based) sample the
[DOA](#id1) space with a resolution of $`5\text{ degrees}`$.

### 5.1 Impact of Binary Frequency Selection on [DOA](#id1) Estimation

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 4: Frame-wise psACC results over the [DOA](#id1) for different
reverberation times in test-1S (only the central frame where $`n=50`$
was used for evaluation to ensure speech activity). The square
represents a $`T_{60}`$ of $`0.16`$ s, the triangle of $`0.36`$ s, and
the circle of $`0.61`$ s. In the left column, B-FM/B-OM was applied such
that only 50 randomly selected frequency bands were used. In the right
column, B-FM/B-OM was applied for different frequency ranges (FRs), from
$`k=0`$ to $`k=50`$, from $`k=100`$ to $`k=150`$, and from $`k=200`$ to
$`k=250`$ were evaluated. In the respective scenarios, only frequency
bands in the respective range were used.

The effect of attention in terms of masking on the DDNNs has not yet
been studied in depth. In particular, it is not clear what effect
different attention distributions have on the DDNN performance/whether
there is a bias in the DDNN towards specific attention distributions. To
investigate the effect in a controlled way, we evaluate two different
attention distributions represented by binary masks that contain $`50`$
ones and $`257-50=207`$ zeros per time frame. In a file with multiple
time-frames, the mask is the same for all time-frames. In the first
attention distribution, the ones are selected randomly via a uniform
distribution per file. In the second attention distribution, the ones
are selected deterministically. We refer to these attention
distributions as attention-distribution one and
attention-distribution two, respectively. We distinguish three different
binary masking procedures, (I) random phase-masking (rB-PM) and (II)
random feature-masking (rB-FM) using attention-distribution one and
(III) deterministic feature-masking (dB-FM) using
attention-distribution two, where the binary mask contains ones in the
frequency bands from 100 to 150. The results are summarized in
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms").
The results in this section are based on the single-source data set
test-1S and the DDNNs are trained with train-1S.

If no masking (i.e., $`M=1`$) is applied, all methods (except Model 6)
achieve a psACC higher than or equal to $`80\%`$ in
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")
in the presence of noise and reverberation. The signal-processing
methods perform comparably to the deep-learning methods; see Models 2,
5, and 15, 16. Using the inter-microphone phase-differences as input
instead of the raw phases does not result in better performance for the
broadband [CNN](#id7)-based DDNNs. The phase difference input only
improves the results for the DDNNs based solely on feed-forward layers.
This shows that [CNN](#id7)s can denoise the input better than
[FFNN](#id9)s. In particular, Model 5, which uses the raw phase as
input, performs best in terms of ACC and MAE. A possible explanation is
the additional convolution layer of the [CNN](#id7)s, which use the raw
phases instead of the phase differences as input that increases the
learning capabilities of the DDNN. Batch normalization between the
[CNN](#id7) layers does not influence the results, as the performance of
Models 1 and 5 is comparable to the performance of Models 3 and 7.

When masking is applied, rB-FM outperforms rB-PM consistently, as in
\[[48](#bib.bib48)\]. The results show that if only feed-forward layers
are used, the performance drops when any type of masking is applied, as
can be seen in the rB-PM column of Models 9 and 11. Consequently, we
exclude these models from further evaluations. Using rB-FM, the
narrowband models perform worse than the broadband models. Therefore,
having inter-frequency connections in the DDNN helps to estimate the
[DOA](#id1), especially given noisy inputs. Interestingly, using the
phase differences instead of the phases as input improves the
performance for the narrowband models. For dB-FM, the narrowband models
fail completely. Also, the performance of the broadband models is
strongly degraded, although having access to the same number of
frequency bins as when using rB-FM. The performance degradation is much
less severe for signal processing-based methods like MUSIC or SRP-P.
This effect can be explained by [DNN](#id6) training. The DDNNs have
been trained with spatiotemporally white noise and directional
temporally white noise. On a short time-frame basis ($`\approx 32`$ ms),
the addition of two white noise processes leads to time-frequency bins
where the relative energy of directional and non-directional noise can
vary strongly, meaning that time-frequency bins where the directional
noise source is dominant are uniformly distributed over the frequencies.
This distribution is resembled by rB-FM, where the bin-wise SNR for
masked bins (i.e., unattended) can be assumed to be
$`-\rotatebox{90.0}{8}`$ dB, corresponding to the time-frequency bins
dominated by the non-directional noise during training. Consequently,
the bin-wise SNR distribution during testing is very different when
employing dB-FM compared to the uniform bin-wise SNR distribution during
training.

To investigate the effect further, we plot the psACC on a frame-basis
over the [DOA](#id1) and for different reverberation times in
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.1 Impact of Binary Frequency Selection on Estimation ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")
for selected models. For rB-FM, on the left side, the performance of the
DDNNs and SRP-P deteriorates slightly. Please note the bias to
$`90^{\circ}`$ is typical for a ULA. For dB-FM, shown on the right side
of
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.1 Impact of Binary Frequency Selection on Estimation ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
the DDNNs fail to estimate specific directions correctly, completely for
all tested reverberation times. However, the results of SRP-P do not
exhibit such complete failures for specific [DOA](#id1)s for different
frequency distributions. The performance of the DDNNs deteriorates for
all three considered frequency-band ranges in dB-FM compared to rB-FM,
although having the same number of frequency bands to estimate the
[DOA](#id1) from. Remarkably, when using dB-FM, the performance
deterioration of the DDNNs is [DOA](#id1) and frequency-band range
dependent. For specific [DOA](#id1)s and band ranges, e.g., band range
100-150, $`60^{\circ}`$ [DOA](#id1),
$`\text{FFNN}_{\Delta P}^{\text{N}}`$, the psACC drops to almost 0,
whereas for other [DOA](#id1)s, e.g., $`15^{\circ}`$, the performance is
comparable to no masking. This effect is especially prominent for the
narrowband model, less for the broadband model, and again less for SRP-P
as it did not require any training. Consequently, having access to all
frequencies as the broadband model provides more reliable [DOA](#id1)
estimates. Based on these findings, we exclude the narrowband estimators
from further evaluations and investigate training for speech.
Additionally, the performance gap between dB-FM and rB-FM suggests that
training the DDNNs with the signal class to estimate the [DOA](#id1)
from and with the spectral attention distribution used in the test
instead of uniformly distributed noise can further improve the
performance. We further evaluate this hypothesis in the next section.
