Here we compare different training strategies for the [DOA](#id1) and
attention modules in the presence of two sources (a directional speech
and a directional interference source) and noise. For fully
[DNN](#id6)-based [DOA](#id1) estimation, we evaluate attention
application in the form of the proposed R-FM and R-PM and compare to
R-PM\* \[[44](#bib.bib44)\]. Training strategies include: (I) Training
the ADNN and the DDNN jointly E2E using the [CCE](#id2) loss for the
[DOA](#id1) label of speech with train-2s (see Equation
([17](#S3.E17 "In 3.2.1 End-to-End Training With Feature or Phase Masking ‣ 3.2 Attention Module and Training Strategies ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))).
(II) Training the DDNN on a time-frame basis with directional noise
sources from train-1S \[[38](#bib.bib38)\], freezing the DDNN weights
and training the ADNN E2E using train-2s and the [CCE](#id2) loss with
the [DOA](#id1) label of speech (see Equation
([17](#S3.E17 "In 3.2.1 End-to-End Training With Feature or Phase Masking ‣ 3.2 Attention Module and Training Strategies ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))).
(III) Training an ADNN with the MSE for speech enhancement and combining
it with the DDNNs from (I) and (II). (IV) Training the DDNN without
attention using train-2s and the [CCE](#id2) loss with the [DOA](#id1)
label of speech. (see Equation
([17](#S3.E17 "In 3.2.1 End-to-End Training With Feature or Phase Masking ‣ 3.2 Attention Module and Training Strategies ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))).
(V) Training the DDNN without attention and directional noise sources
\[[38](#bib.bib38)\]. For hybrid systems, we compare ADNNs combined with
SRP-MP trained using the MSE, or the PSM for speech enhancement with the
proposed training based on the [SPS](#id10) using train-2s. We refer to
the respective methods via SRP-P (MSE), SRP-P (PSM), SRP-P (SPS),
respectively. The evaluation was performed using data simulated with
measured RIRs using test-2S. Note that the ground-truth label is only
based on the [DOA](#id1) of the [SOI](#id5). Unless specified
differently, the used DDNN is $`\text{CNN}^{\tiny{B}}_{\tiny{P}}`$.

In
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.2 Impact of Training Data and Attention Application on Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
we report results for the different training strategies for the DDNN.
The worst results are expected with training strategies (IV) and (V) as
no attention is applied. The DDNN trained with noise in (V) cannot
decide whether to focus on the speech or the noise source but estimates
the [DOA](#id1)s of both sources. By chance, either the speech or the
noise [DOA](#id1) is picked in the evaluation (see, for example, the red
line of the [CNN](#id7) in
Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5.2 Impact of Training Data and Attention Application on Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")).
Note that (V) only serves as an anchor that puts the results into
perspective. As it is not performing signal-aware [DOA](#id1)
estimation, it does not serve as a baseline. When training with speech
in (IV) instead of noise, the DDNN seems to learn speech-specific
structures in the phase map such that the [DOA](#id1) of the speech
source is more prominent than the [DOA](#id1) of the noise source. As a
result, when training the DDNN with speech rather than noise, the MAE is
reduced from $`37.9^{\circ}`$ to $`16.7^{\circ}`$ when no mask is
applied. Consequently, the DDNN learned speech-specific characteristics
from the input to be biased to speech sources. Note that no magnitude
information is used here. This bias cannot be learned when training with
spatiotemporally white Gaussian noise \[[38](#bib.bib38)\] as in (V).

When additional attention in the form of R-PM, R-PM\*, or R-FM is
applied, the results improve further. The best performance is achieved
using the proposed R-FM. The application of R-FM yields better results
than R-PM\* \[[44](#bib.bib44)\]. This shows that the masking of
features after the [CNN](#id7) layers is superior to masking the input.
Interestingly, the DDNN achieves better results for R-PM\* compared to
R-PM. When the mask is zero at some bins in R-PM\*, this corresponds to
a [DOA](#id1) of $`90^{\circ}`$ assuming the DDNN learns a physical
model. The additional noise included by the unlearnable phase
randomization of R-PM seems to deteriorate the results more severely
than the deviation of the physical model when using R-PM\*. This result
and the strong discrepancy between the DDNN performance for rB-FM and
dB-FM in
Section [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Impact of Binary Frequency Selection on Estimation ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")
show that the DDNN does not learn an exact physical model. Instead, it
learns the mapping from input to the [DOA](#id1) that optimizes the loss
based on the training data.

In
Table [5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.2 Impact of Training Data and Attention Application on Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
we report the results of different training methods for the ADNN, namely
the MSE
([4](#S2.E4 "In 2.2.1 Architecture and Training ‣ 2.2 Fully -Based Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")),
the PSM
([8](#S2.E8 "In 2.3 Baseline System: Hybrid Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))
and with the respective [DOA](#id1) module using the SPS loss for SRP-MP
([19](#S3.E19 "In 3.2.3 DOA-Based Training using SRP-MP ‣ 3.2 Attention Module and Training Strategies ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))
and [E2E](#id3) for the DDNN
([17](#S3.E17 "In 3.2.1 End-to-End Training With Feature or Phase Masking ‣ 3.2 Attention Module and Training Strategies ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")).
All methods improve the result compared to the attention-free scenarios.
For SRP-MP, training the ADNN with a localization loss yields slightly
better results than training with the MSE. Training with the PSM further
minimizes the gap. This can be explained as the PSM takes the phase into
account, which is important for source localization. Additionally, the
MSE weights mask differences with the mixture magnitude. This increases
the weight of low frequencies if the [SOI](#id5) is speech, although
higher frequencies allow for more accurate localization. For the DDNN,
[E2E](#id3) training is more important, as the MSE mask yields an MAE of
$`24.5^{\circ}`$, and the [E2E](#id3) mask an MAE of $`6.2^{\circ}`$.
Note that the computational complexity of SRP-MP is much less than for
the DDNN, but the performance is comparable. Also, SRP-MP does not have
a bias towards the respective training source in the [DOA](#id1) module
in contrast to the DDNN.

Especially interesting is the small performance difference for SRP-MP
when a PSM or an [SPS](#id10) mask is used. In terms of dual-use, this
approach allows using independently trained source
separation/enhancement/extraction ADNNs with signal processing-based
methods for [DOA](#id1) estimation without strong performance
degradation in terms of [DOA](#id1) estimation compared to [SPS](#id10)
training or [E2E](#id3) training using the DDNN. Another advantage of
the SRP-MP (PSM) approach is the independence of the training data of
the array architecture, as only an ADNN and no DDNN is used. When DDNNs
are used, retraining is required for every new array architecture,
whereas with SRP-MP, the SRP-P model can be adjusted w.r.t. the array
architecture. Additionally, when the ADNN is trained with the PSM, it is
sufficient to simulate training data for a single microphone and not for
an array, which reduces the overall computational burden when
SRP-MP (PSM) is trained. Furthermore, when training the ADNN with the
MSE/PSM, the signal processing-based method can be used as a black box
and does not have to be implemented in a differentiable way. An
advantage of the DDNN is that it only requires the [DOA](#id1) label of
the [SOI](#id5) for training such that it could be trained with measured
data if the ground-truth [DOA](#id1) is provided, e.g., by an optical
tracking system. In contrast, all investigated training objectives for
the ADNN using SRP-MP require a representation of the [SOI](#id5) at the
first microphone, which complicates training using measured data.

Figure 6: Results of MAE, ACC, and psACC of B-FM \[[48](#bib.bib48)\]
and SRP-MP. The ADNN is trained with the MSE
([4](#S2.E4 "In 2.2.1 Architecture and Training ‣ 2.2 Fully -Based Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))
for a speech enhancement objective and the DDNN is trained with noise
\[[38](#bib.bib38)\]. Note that the psACC is always higher than the ACC.
The black lines mark the results of R-FM from

In
Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5.2 Impact of Training Data and Attention Application on Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
we show the [DOA](#id1) estimation performance based on SRP-MP
coefficients and based on a DDNN with the respective attention masks.
Training [E2E](#id3)/with the [SPS](#id10) yields different masks that
cannot be used for an enhancement objective. For example, the masks
trained with the speech enhancement objective clearly exhibit the
magnitude structure of speech at lower frequencies, whereas the masks
trained for localization do not. Especially interesting are the
differences between the masks obtained with the [SPS](#id10) training
for SRP-MP and the [E2E](#id3) training with the DDNN. Where the
SRP-MP (SPS) mask is relatively sparse, the DDNN mask is not. In the
DDNN, all frequency bands are connected and yield a single estimate per
time frame. SRP-MP can be interpreted as estimating a [DOA](#id1) per
frequency bin and averaging these estimates. In the DDNN case, the
internal connection seems to require rather non-sparse inputs, whereas
the averaging of SRP-MP (SPS) seems to select only a few time-frames but
then nearly all of the respective frequency bins. A comparison of the
masks of SRP-MP (SPS) and SRP-MP (MSE) shows that SRP-MP (SPS) yields
masks that focus on the low-reverberant speech onsets. The SRP-MP (MSE)
mask is between the SRP-MP (SPS) and the DDNN masks in terms of
sparsity. The SRP-MP coefficients of MSE and [SPS](#id10) masks look
very similar, although the respective masks are quite different. This
shows the robustness of SRP-MP w.r.t. different input masks. The DDNN
estimates look sharper than the SRP-MP estimates. The DDNN was trained
to have sharp outputs and prior information of an angular separation of
sources larger than $`5^{\circ}`$ from the training data, whereas SRP-MP
is model-based and not optimized to yield such sharp outputs. The
different output representations, consequently, may be misleading in
terms of selecting the best algorithm. This is justified as the
respective ACC, psACC, and MAE results are very comparable for the DDNN
and SRP-MP in
Table [5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.2 Impact of Training Data and Attention Application on Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms").

In
Figure [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 5.2 Impact of Training Data and Attention Application on Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
we report the results of B-FM as in \[[48](#bib.bib48)\] over
$`v_{\text{thr}}`$ for a DDNN trained with noise with train-1S and an
ADNN trained with the MSE
([4](#S2.E4 "In 2.2.1 Architecture and Training ‣ 2.2 Fully -Based Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))
with train-2S. Note that the results differ from \[[48](#bib.bib48)\],
as the ADNN is a two-layer LSTM instead of a three-layer BLSTM, the file
length is different ($`1.6`$ instead of $`3~s`$). We use the same binary
mask with SRP-MP (MSE) to see whether binary or ratio masks are
advantageous for SRP-MP (MSE). We compare the results to the DDNN. The
DDNN achieves the best performance at $`v_{\text{thr}}\approx 0.2`$. In
total, the ACC is improved from $`42`$ to $`59`$ %, and the MAE is
reduced from $`38^{\circ}`$ to $`14.9^{\circ}`$ for the DDNN. For
SRP-MP, the best performance is achieved at
$`v_{\text{thr}}\approx 0.4`$ when the MAE is reduced from
$`39^{\circ}`$ to $`6.2^{\circ}`$. This result is the same for the best
model, the DDNN, with [E2E](#id3) training in
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.2 Impact of Training Data and Attention Application on Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms").
The ACC of SRP-MP, however, is still $`9`$ % percent worse compared to
the [E2E](#id3) trained DDNN. The psACC of both is comparable with
$`79`$ to $`83`$ %. The performance gap of DDNN and SRP-MP in
Figure [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 5.2 Impact of Training Data and Attention Application on Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")
shows that DDNNs are more sensitive to attention than SRP-MP. As signal
processing-based methods for [DOA](#id1) estimation are typically not
tailored to any source class or array architecture, unlike DDNNs and
their computational complexity is typically less than that of DDNNs, we
believe that the combination ADNNs for attention and signal
processing-based methods for [DOA](#id1) estimation constitutes a
low-complexity solution with high psACC and low MAE.

### 5.3 Evaluation of Off-Grid [DOA](#id1)s

Figure 7: Off-grid median+95% confidence interval (upper plot) and
mean+standard deviation (lower plot) evaluation of the [AE](#id11). The
DDNN is trained [E2E](#id3) using R-FM with a [DOA](#id1) resolution of
$`5^{\circ}`$. SRP-MP is trained using the [SPS](#id10) with the
resolution of $`5^{\circ}`$. In SRP-MP-FG, the same ADNN is used as for
SRP-MP, but the resolution of the [DOA](#id1) module is increased in the
test to match the [DOA](#id1) resolution of the simulated sources
($`\frac{180}{179}^{\circ}`$).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 8: Excerpt of the confusion matrix from $`0`$ to $`85`$ degrees
of the [DOA](#id1) labels vs. the estimated [DOA](#id1)s of the
DDNN (top) and SRP-MP (bottom). The estimated [DOA](#id1)s have a
resolution of 5 degrees and the labels of 1 degree. The evaluated
two-source data set is similar to test-2S-HR; only the label resolution
was changed from $`\frac{180}{179}^{\circ}`$ to $`1^{\circ}`$ for
visualization purposes.

In the previous experiments using test-2S, the [SOI](#id5) [DOA](#id1)s
were matched to the directions that the [DOA](#id1) modules sample. As
all the evaluated [DOA](#id1) estimation algorithms sample the
[DOA](#id1) space, such an on-grid comparison is fair in the sense that
no method has an advantage over the other. Also, the use of measured
RIRs for data simulation inherently leads to slight off-grid positions,
e.g., due to measurement or microphone placement errors. However,
stronger off-grid [DOA](#id1)s of the sources-of-interest lead to
additional rounding errors and consequently to an increased MAE.
Additionally, as DDNNs learn an input to output mapping, it is not
inherently clear whether they generalize to off-grid [DOA](#id1)s.

In this section, we show that the proposed methods generalize to
off-grid [DOA](#id1)s. As the baseline in \[[54](#bib.bib54)\] uses a
signal processing method for [DOA](#id1) estimation and the baseline in
\[[44](#bib.bib44)\] uses the same [DOA](#id1) [DNN](#id6) architecture
as $`\text{CNN}^{\tiny{B}}_{\tiny{P}}`$, the results for off-grid
[DOA](#id1)s can be transferred to the respective methods and are not
shown here. We evaluate the effect of off-grid [DOA](#id1)s on the
signal-aware [DOA](#id1) estimation performance using the two-source
data set test-2S-HR. The ADNNs are trained [E2E](#id3)/using the SPS
with the respective [DOA](#id1) module using train-2S. We show the
results of the MAE and the median absolute-error (MedAE) over the
[DOA](#id1) in
Figure [7](#S5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 5.3 Evaluation of Off-Grid s ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
where the [DOA](#id1) space is sampled with a 5 degree resolution, and
the ground-truth [DOA](#id1) of the sources-of-interest is between 0 and
180 degree on 180 grid points (angular distance between two grid points
is $`\frac{180}{179}`$ degree). A decreased performance of the MAE and
the MedAE can be observed around 0 degree, as expected for a ULA. Over
the [DOA](#id1), the MedAE exhibits a clear triangular structure with
the highest MedAE in between the sampling points of the [DOA](#id1)
modules. The MAE and the standard deviation, however, do not exhibit
such a clear structure. The high ACC and psACC reported in the previous
experiments, the MedAE structure with the 95% confidence interval and
the standard deviation of the MAE suggest that the MAE is mostly
dominated by outliers such that no clear on/off-grid structure can be
observed as in the MedAE plot. In addition to SRP-MP (SPS) and
$`\text{CNN}^{\tiny{B}}_{\tiny{P}}`$ with a 5 degree sampling
resolution, we also evaluate SRP-MP (SPS) with a
$`\frac{180}{179}`$ degree sampling resolution to show the flexibility
of the approach (during training, the [DOA](#id1) resolution was
5 degree). Such a change is not possible for DDNNs without the necessity
to change the number of output classes of the DDNN architecture and
retraining. The increased [DOA](#id1) sampling resolution for
SRP-MP (SPS) leads to a reduced MedAE and MAE. This shows that
scenario-dependent modifications of the [DOA](#id1) module can be
performed after training if the [DOA](#id1) module is a
signal-processing method.

To investigate the effect of off-grid sources further, an excerpt of an
estimate vs. actual [DOA](#id1) confusion plot is shown in
Figure [8](#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5.3 Evaluation of Off-Grid s ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms").
It is shown that for SRP-MP (SPS) and for
$`\text{CNN}^{\tiny{B}}_{\tiny{P}}`$, the estimated [DOA](#id1) of
off-grid sources is typically the closest [DOA](#id1) that can be
estimated due to the discrete sampling resolution of 5 degrees of the
estimators. If a source [DOA](#id1) is in the middle of two sampled
[DOA](#id1)s, the algorithms choose either of the neighboring classes.
Both algorithms show comparable performance. Around 0 degree, as
expected for a ULA, the algorithms perform worse (the [DOA](#id1)-based
changes in inter-microphone phase-differences have a sine dependency;
the sine is zero at 0 degree, which hinders the [DOA](#id1) estimation).

Please note that the overall results in this experiment are better
compared to the previous experiments, irrespective of the off-grid
evaluation due to the use of simulated RIRs here. Additionally,
SRP-MP (SPS) performs better than the DDNN with an MAE of
$`3.6^{\circ}`$ for the coarse and of $`2.9^{\circ}`$ for the fine-grid
evaluation compared to an MAE of $`4.6^{\circ}`$ for the DDNN. Physical
model violations due to the use of measured RIRs with slight microphone
perturbations seem to influence the performance of SRP-MP stronger than
of the DDNN. Similar results have been found in \[[38](#bib.bib38)\] for
SRP-P.

Figure 10: [DOA](#id1) estimates of measured data using the respective
methods. In a), the raw outputs are shown, whereas in b) the raw outputs
are averaged over 0.4 s, respectively. There is a single moving speech
source active tracked via an OptiTrack (orange line). There are
additional directional interfering sources moving from 180 to 0 degrees
as can be seen in SRP without attention. The SIR was lower than
$`-4.5`$ dB. For SRP-MP (SPS), the ADNN was trained with either $`N=30`$
or $`N=100`$ frames.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 11: [AE](#id11) per time-frame between the estimated and the
ground-truth [DOA](#id1) obtained via an OptiTrack. The figure
demonstrates the number of reliable time-frames per method. For each
method, the time-frames are ordered from low AE to high AE irrespective
of the output energy in the respective [DOA](#id1) estimate (see
Figure [10](#S5.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 5.4 Outlook: Evaluation using Measured Data of Moving Sources ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")).
Methods with very sparse outputs consequently have a very fast
increasing AE curve. There are no abrupt increases of the AE as the high
number of evaluated time-frames leads to a smooth AE curve. The SIR was
smaller than $`-4.5`$ dB.

Finally, we compare $`\text{CNN}^{\tiny{B}}_{\tiny{P}}`$, SRP-MP (SPS)
and SRP-MP (PSM) using measured data for one moving speaker (the
[SOI](#id5)), with undesired directional sources, and diffuse background
sounds with a SIR smaller than $`-4.5`$ dB
(room size: 4.7 m, 4.87 m, 2.6 m height; $`T_{60}`$: 0.5 s). A plot of
the recorded signals can be seen in
Figure [9](#S5.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ 5.4 Outlook: Evaluation using Measured Data of Moving Sources ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms").
The ground-truth source positions were obtained using an optical
tracking system \[[85](#bib.bib85)\]. The outputs of the estimators are
visualized in
Figure [10](#S5.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 5.4 Outlook: Evaluation using Measured Data of Moving Sources ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")
(not normalized). The output of SRP-P shows a stationary directional
interfering source at approximately $`95{{}^{\circ}}`$ and moving
directional interfering sources. The [DOA](#id1) of the speech source is
barely visible. Such an output is expected if no attention is applied.
The output of SRP-MP (SPS) is temporally very sparse, however, the
estimates are very close to the ground truth obtained via optical
tracking. This result is consistent with the sparse masks of
SRP-MP (SPS) seen in
Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5.2 Impact of Training Data and Attention Application on Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms").
In this low-SIR environment, SRP-MP (SPS) only bases the [DOA](#id1)
estimates on very few time-frames that yield very accurate estimates.
This effect can be explained via the objective function
([19](#S3.E19 "In 3.2.3 DOA-Based Training using SRP-MP ‣ 3.2 Attention Module and Training Strategies ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")),
where the estimated [SPS](#id10) is optimized to resemble the
[SPS](#id10) of the ground-truth, both after normalization (see
([14](#S2.E14 "In 2.3 Baseline System: Hybrid Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 2 Fundamentals ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))).
The normalization removes the energy-diminishing effects of the
mask/attention such that a very sparse mask can still yield a very low
loss. Such sparse estimates are acceptable for static or slowly moving
sources, however, not for tracking moving sources or a very short
temporal context.

An additional experiment was conducted to study the influence of the
length $`N`$of the training context window on the output. We expect that
the outputs are less sparse if SRP-MP (SPS) is trained with shorter
context windows ($`N=30`$ instead of $`N=100`$ time-frames, during
training), denoted as SRP-MP (SPS) $`N=30`$. As shown in
Figure [10](#S5.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 5.4 Outlook: Evaluation using Measured Data of Moving Sources ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
the outputs of SRP-MP (SPS) $`N=30`$ are less sparse than of
SRP-MP (SPS) at the cost of reduced performance on test-2S (79 %, 67 %,
8.7 ^(∘), for psACC, ACC, MAE, respectively). SRP-MP (SPS) yields
sharper outputs than SRP-MP (PSM) in
Figure [10](#S5.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 5.4 Outlook: Evaluation using Measured Data of Moving Sources ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms").
However, SRP-MP (PSM) also yields less sparse outputs than SRP-MP (SPS).
The outputs are temporally less sparse as the ADNN was trained to
resemble the PSM that is defined on a time-frequency bin-basis.
Less-sparse outputs are advantageous for tracking. Interestingly, as
shown in
Table [5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.2 Impact of Training Data and Attention Application on Signal-Aware Estimation ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"),
the sharper outputs of SRP-MP (SPS) improve the ACC only by 2 % compared
to SRP-MP (PSM). The DDNN yields very narrow non-sparse estimates that
are very close to the path of the speech source. In contrast to
SRP-MP (SPS), the outputs are not sparse as the ADNN objective in
([17](#S3.E17 "In 3.2.1 End-to-End Training With Feature or Phase Masking ‣ 3.2 Attention Module and Training Strategies ‣ 3 Proposed Frequency-Selective Estimation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms"))
does not exhibit a normalization of the estimates. The non-sparse
outputs make the DDNN more suited for tracking than SRP-MP (SPS).

All methods also generalize to measured data under low SIR/SNR
conditions and moving sources. The outputs of SRP-MP (PSM) are much
broader than those of the DDNN. We compare the frame-wise [AE](#id11)
(reordered time-frames) of the respective file in
Figure [11](#S5.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ 5.4 Outlook: Evaluation using Measured Data of Moving Sources ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")
to investigate whether this is a visualization issue only. As expected,
SRP-MP (SPS) and SRP-MP (SPS) $`N=30`$ exhibit very few frames with a
low error as the estimated outputs are temporally very sparse.
SRP-MP (SPS) $`N=30`$ has a lower AE for more time-frames, as expected.
The DDNN and SRP-MP (PSM) perform comparably for approximately 400
frames before the AE of the DDNN begins to increase rapidly.
Consequently, the broad lobes of SRP-MP (PSM) are misleading in terms of
frame-wise MAE for a single [SOI](#id5). As multi-source localization of
sparse sources (like speech) can be broken down to single-source
localization, the broad lobes of SRP-MP (SPS) pose no disadvantage for
localization.
Figure [10](#S5.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 5.4 Outlook: Evaluation using Measured Data of Moving Sources ‣ 5 Performance Evaluation ‣ Signal-Aware Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using Attention Mechanisms")
shows that both the DDNN and SRP-MP (PSM) are suited for tracking as
there are temporally non-sparse estimates that follow the [SOI](#id5)
path.

As all methods estimate the [DOA](#id1) on an [STFT](#id4) time-frame
basis, an extension to more sophisticated source tracking can be
achieved, for example, by using recurrent neural networks or particle
filters that process the frame-wise [DOA](#id1) estimates of the
proposed and baseline methods (see, e.g., \[[43](#bib.bib43)\]). For
tracking, temporally non-sparse estimates are beneficial if a high
temporal [DOA](#id1) resolution is required; for this, SRP-MP (SPS) is
less suited than SRP-MP (PSM). Finally, the DDNN and SRP-MP (PSM) both
seem to be suited for tracking. As SRP-MP (PSM) has an overall lower
computational complexity than the DDNN and performs comparable in all
tests, we conclude that hybrid approaches represent a low complexity,
high flexibility, highly accurate method for signal-aware [DOA](#id1)
estimation.

## 6 Conclusion

We used a [DNN](#id6) to estimate attention from a single-channel
microphone spectrum. The attention was subsequently used in a fully
[DNN](#id6)-based system or a hybrid fashion in signal processing-based
methods for signal-aware [DOA](#id1) estimation of speech sources. We
showed that spectral context is crucial for [DNN](#id6)-based
[DOA](#id1) estimators and that they are biased towards the source
classes and the attention distribution seen during training. In
contrast, signal processing-based [DOA](#id1) estimation does not
exhibit such a bias. We proposed [DOA](#id1)-based training objectives
for fully data-driven and hybrid signal-aware [DOA](#id1) estimators and
showed that both variants perform comparably. We also showed that the
spectrum of a single microphone is sufficient to compute attention,
making the attention computation independent of the array architecture,
assuming a signal-processing method is used for subsequent [DOA](#id1)
estimation. This is especially interesting as, in contrast to
[DNN](#id6)s, signal-processing methods can be modified and adapted
during runtime without retraining the attention estimator to match
different conditions, like array architectures, inter-microphone
distances, number of microphones, etc. We conclude that hybrid systems
pose a low complexity, high flexibility approach for signal-aware
[DOA](#id1) estimation with comparable performance to fully
[DNN](#id6)-based signal-aware [DOA](#id1) estimation.
